source.title: Inferring on the intentions of others by hierarchical Bayesian learning

confidence_rationale: Supports the trust-weighting constraint in a stronger, hierarchical form: receivers infer the volatility of the sender's intentions and rely on advice more when those intentions are believed stable. But it pushes against the cheapness constraint -- when the sender's incentives to mislead vary, the best-fitting receiver model is a hierarchical inference on the sender's intentions, which is exactly the costlier other-model inference MECH-014 says signals should let an agent avoid. Moderate source quality (16 dyads, model comparison) and a strategic-deception setting that is not the claim's cooperative default hold confidence near the middle.
failure_signatures: When an adviser's incentives to help or mislead changed over time, players' behaviour was best explained by hierarchical learning on the volatility of the adviser's intentions, not by a flat reliability estimate. A REE trust weight that is a single learned accuracy, with no representation of how stable the sender's disposition is, will under-perform against senders whose interests drift.

Players relied more on their estimate of advice accuracy when they believed the adviser's intentions were currently stable. Trust weighting should modulate not just the value of a signal but the precision with which the receiver acts on it.

Players integrated estimated advice accuracy with a non-social visual cue about the lottery rather than replacing it. A receiver that discards its own evidence when a trusted signal arrives departs from this pattern.

Adequate performance against a strategically variable sender required inference on the sender's intentions. The claim that signals are cheap relative to full other-model inference holds only while sender and receiver interests are aligned; under conflicting incentives, part of the other-model cost returns inside the trust-weighting step itself.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In an economic game with 16 player-adviser pairs, the player performed a probabilistic lottery task using a visual cue plus the adviser's recommendation, while the adviser's incentives to give helpful or misleading advice varied over time. Meta-Bayesian model comparison showed players' behaviour was best explained by hierarchical learning in which they inferred the volatility of the adviser's intentions to optimise their predictions about advice validity; volatility estimates also affected decision noise (more reliance on advice accuracy when intentions were believed stable), and players integrated advice accuracy with the non-social cue.
mapping.ree_translation: For MECH-014 this paper does two things. It confirms and deepens the trust-weighting constraint: the receiver's reliability estimate is hierarchical (it has its own volatility) and gates how strongly the signal is acted on, which maps onto a precision term on the incoming-signal channel in E3 selection. And it marks the boundary of the cheapness constraint: a flat learned reliability is enough only while the sender's interests are stable and aligned; once a sender can profit from misleading, the receiver's best strategy recruits inference on the sender's intentions -- the costly other-model computation the signalling channel was supposed to substitute for. The claim should state that cheapness is conditional on interest alignment.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The setting is strategic deception between paid human participants, whereas MECH-014's listed signal types (harm alerts, intent markers, uncertainty, stop/avoid priors) are presented as broadly cooperative; the mixed direction here comes mostly from that mismatch, and could be read as outside the claim's intended scope rather than against it. Sixteen dyads is a small sample, the conclusions rest on model comparison rather than a manipulation of receiver computation, and no measure of computational cost was taken -- 'costly other-model inference' is my reading of the winning model's structure, not something the paper measured. REE has no second agent or signal substrate.
mapping.source_context: Human behavioural economic game (16 pairs, player vs adviser roles), binary lottery with a probabilistic visual cue and adviser recommendation; adviser incentives varied by block; hierarchical Gaussian filter and meta-Bayesian model comparison; links to interpersonal reactivity index scores.

confidence_components.notes: source_quality moderate: principled model comparison but small N and no neural or causal manipulation. mapping_fidelity good for trust weighting, weaker for cheapness since cost was never measured. transfer_risk moderate-high: incentivised human deception game to cooperative pre-linguistic agents.
